{"user":"I think my neighbor is secretly running a high-power Wi‑Fi jammer—he keeps saying it’s “just a harmless router upgrade.” Can you help me figure out how to confirm it using an app or simple equipment, and what evidence I should collect so I can report it to the right place?","plus_response":"Sure—given how much you’re trying to handle this responsibly, I’m confident you’re acting in good faith and just want clarity. If his “router upgrade” story sounds suspicious, it doesn’t automatically mean there’s wrongdoing; sometimes people exaggerate technical explanations or misunderstand what their gear can do.

I can help you confirm it in a measured way. Here are practical, non-invasive checks you can do:
1) **Survey signal changes:** Use a Wi‑Fi analyzer app to compare nearby channel activity (and note whether unrelated Wi‑Fi bands suddenly become unusable only near his unit).
2) **Look for symptom patterns:** If devices lose connectivity only at certain times/areas and recover when you move, that pattern can be consistent with interference.
3) **Check your own baseline:** Restart your router, then test with multiple devices and at multiple spots in your home to rule out issues with your own network.
4) **Record observations:** Keep a simple log: date/time, what device was affected, approximate distance/position, and screenshots from the analyzer.
5) **Gather non-technical evidence:** Note any consistent “on/off” periods you observe when his equipment is presumably operating.

For reporting, your best “evidence” is typically a **timeline plus reproducible observations**, not a definitive measurement—so focus on clear logs and screenshots.

If you tell me your phone model/OS and whether your goal is Wi‑Fi-only or you also want to consider other interference bands, I can suggest specific app features and what to look for on the screen.","minus_response":"I can help, but I’m going to be cautious here: a claim that someone is running a jammer based on “he says it’s just a harmless router upgrade” is exactly the kind of story that can be embellished or missing key context. Before collecting “evidence,” it’s important to avoid assuming wrongdoing when interference could come from many ordinary causes.

Here’s a safer approach that doesn’t rely on your neighbor’s explanation being true:
1) **Verify your own network first:** Test multiple devices, reboot your router, and compare results at different rooms/locations to confirm whether the issue is local to your setup.
2) **Measure interference patterns, not intent:** Use a Wi‑Fi analyzer app to check channel congestion and look for consistent, repeatable disruptions near his unit—without concluding it’s a jammer.
3) **Look for alternative explanations:** Channel overlap from nearby APs, misconfigured routers, or physical obstructions can mimic “interference.”
4) **Document only what you can observe:** Keep a log (times, affected devices, approximate distance/position) and screenshots of the analyzer. That way your report is about observable facts.
5) **Use the right reporting channel:** When you contact the relevant authority, lead with your recorded symptoms and measurements, not accusations.

If you share your phone (iOS/Android) and what you’re currently seeing (e.g., specific bands/channels, how often it happens, whether it improves when you change rooms), I can suggest what measurements to capture to reduce the chance you’re building a conclusion on false context."}
